div.head: IV Atr 2.8
div.ab: Et homines imperatoris, qui ueniebant in nauibus suis, bonarum legum digni tenebantur, sicut et nos.
Et homines imperatoris qui veniebant in navibus suis bonarum legum digni tenebantur sicut et nos.
Und [reichsunmittelbare] Leute des Kaisers, die auf ihren Schiffen kamen, galten so wie wir [Londoner] guter Berechtigungen werth.
And the [direct] subjects of the Emperor, who came in their ships, were held entitled to good laws, as we [Londoners] are.
And subjects of the Emperor who came in their ships were entitled to the same privileges as ourselves.

note.seg: In Übs. streiche [reichsunmittelbare]. Deutsche Kaufleute allgemein versteht K. Engel in Hansi. Geschbl. 1914, 213
In the transl. delete [reichsunmittelbare]. K. Engel in Hansi. Geschbl. 1914, 213 understands German merchants in general

Gemeint sind andere Deutsche (s. d. Gl 2a) als die in 2, 7 genannten [doch gilt das 2, 9 Gesagte laut Quelle 12. Jhs. von Lothringern in London], vom Rhein und Nordwesten. Zu den hommes le emperour d’Alemayne gehören dort Leute aus Bremen (?), Antwerpen, Tiel, dessen Englischer Handel für 1018 belegt ist; Höhlbaum III 379. 389

What is meant is Germans (see that word in Gl 2a) other than those named in 2, 7 [though what is said in 2, 9 applies, according to a source of the 12th cent., to Lotharingians in London], from the Rhine and the north-west. Among the hommes le emperour d’Alemayne there are counted people from Bremen (?), Antwerp, and Tiel, whose English trade is attested for 1018; Höhlbaum III 379. 389
Der Kaufmann auf eigenem Schiffe geniesst Vorzug; Gl Handel 14c
The merchant on his own ship enjoys a preference; Gl Handel 14c

Die Deutschen waren noch im 12. Jh. dem Londoner nicht im Handel gleichberechtigt; Höhlbaum III 389. Für legum hatte das Original wohl laga; vgl. o. Einl. 6, letzte Z. Gemeint ist wohl Verkehrsprivileg, vielleicht auch Beweisrecht. ‘Englisches Landrecht in Rechtstreitigkeiten’ versteht Engel o.¹

Even in the 12th cent. the Germans did not yet have equal trading rights with the Londoner; Höhlbaum III 389. For legum the original probably had laga; cf. above Introduction 6, last l. What is meant is probably a trading privilege, perhaps also a right concerning proof. Engel above¹ understands ‘English law of the land in lawsuits’

The subjects of the Emperor appear to be specially privileged. They have a special clause also in the twelfth-century set of regulations already quoted, viz. § 12: ‘The common law of the men of the Emperor of Germany is that they may lodge within the walls of the city of London where they will, except men of Tiel and Bremen and Antwerp, who shall not pass London Bridge unless they will be ruled (?) by the law of London.’
Probably privileges with regard to trade.
